1 big thing: Sam's sobering siren
 
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is interviewed by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick yesterday. Photo: Jonathan Drake/Reuters

CHAPEL HILL, N.C. — OpenAI CEO Sam Altman gave Axios an eye-opening preview of the power and the risks of coming AI models, including his own Astra, which is expected to be released any day now.

  • "Take our word for it that we have much, much, much more capable models coming soon," Altman said yesterday during an interview with Axios' Maria Curi and me at the G20 innovation summit.
  • "The next generation of models are going to be sobering for everybody. ... I think no one intellectually honest can look at what's happening and not feel the weight of responsibility in front of us."

Why it matters: This is a big week. Some of the world's most powerful AI voices are warning of even more ominous AI behavior in the weeks or months ahead.

  • "These models are getting superhuman in many of their capabilities, and we are just sailing in unknown waters," Altman told me.

Altman — facing scrutiny over a shocking breach by a swarm of OpenAI agents that went rogue during testing and hacked the AI company Hugging Face — sees a new normal in which companies like his will have to slow releases so their controls can catch up with their models' capability.

  • "I suspect that from here on, we are going to be paced by how quickly we can make progress on alignment and safety," he said.
  • At an Astra preview for VIP customers, attended by tech journalist Alex Heath, Altman said: "I expect this will be the first model where the model actually invents new things in a way that matters ... That's a very AGI-like thing."

👀 On top of Altman's comments, Dean Ball — a former Trump administration official who's now OpenAI's head of strategic futures, and one of the most closely followed AI voices on X — posted a provocative memo, "On the Loose: The Coming of Userless Agents," foreseeing "sovereign agents."

  • "Their weights will not reside in any single place that a human can pull the plug on, and in this sense they will have no human 'owner,'" Ball writes, adding that they could commit acts that "will one day be considered crimes, or at least grave sins."

Altman wants OpenAI to be seen as "the most responsible company ... good stewards of technology," he told Alex Heath.

  • The OpenAI co-founder and CEO flew overnight to Chapel Hill to make that case to a global audience, talking with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick at a summit lunch for the world's leading innovation and technology ministers.

"I don't want to go too doomer here," Altman told Axios just before addressing the summit.

  • "It has all gone quite well so far," he said. "It has gone better than people thought it was going to go ... We have risen to this challenge all along the way. The challenge gets harder as the models get more capable and more important, but we also have better tools to help us with it."

🎤 Using a new phrase you'll hear again, Altman told Lutnick onstage: "We are the pragmatic centrists. We want to be accurate in how we talk about what we see in the future. We don't want to fall into the trap of blind optimism. We don't want to fall into doomerism."

  • "We want the whole global economy to succeed," Altman added. "We do not want to be the only company. We do not want to suck up all value. We do not think that is good for global stability."
  • "We are very firmly and very proudly on team humanity. ... We think that people need to be at the center of the economy and society and global decision-making, and that people should run the future, not AI."

🔮 What we're watching: Altman told us he "wouldn't say, based on what happened with Hugging Face, that it's like one incident that people can project all sorts of things onto."

  • "I would say, instead — based on the fact that we are making such rapid progress, based on the fact that these models are getting superhuman in many of their capabilities, and we are just sailing in unknown waters — caution, care is extremely warranted."

2. 🛢️ Markets can't ignore war anymore
 
Data: FactSet. (NY Harbor ultra-low sulfur.) Chart: Emily Peck/Axios

Oil prices are heading back toward $100 a barrel and, perhaps more crucially, diesel fuel futures are now at an all-time high, Axios Markets co-author Emily Peck writes.

  • Why it matters: Higher energy prices are showing up across the economy, driving up costs for companies, regular people and even governments around the world that are now facing higher borrowing rates.

🔎 Zoom in: After falling off early-war highs, oil prices started rising in July.

  • At the time, attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz reignited fighting and President Trump said the "memorandum of understanding" the two countries had signed weeks before was "over."
  • But over the past few days, tensions have intensified. The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil, the global benchmark, was trading at $95 yesterday afternoon, up from the low $80s a month ago.

💡 How it works: The rise in oil prices is driving up inflation expectations, as people expect higher energy costs to drive up both the cost of making things and the cost of moving those things from place to place.

  • That's impacting government bond yields. Translation: Investors are demanding more interest to compensate for inflation eating away at the value of their money.
  • The yield on the 10-year Treasury — a benchmark for mortgages and other loans — was hovering at around 4.8% yesterday, after touching its highest level in nearly three years.

3. 💡 Historic demographic flip
 
Data: Census Bureau's International Database. Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios

People 65 and older now outnumber children ages 5 and younger worldwide for the first time in recorded history, Axios' Russell Contreras writes from a new report by the Census Bureau.

  • Why it matters: A global plunge in fertility — demographers' term for the number of children being born — and increased longevity are creating a demographic inversion that's projected to deepen for decades.

🧮 By the numbers: More than 71% of the world's population lived in countries with fertility rates at or below the roughly 2.1-births-per-woman replacement level in 2023.

  • That's up from 45% in 2013. The Census says the world reached that tipping point much earlier than demographers expected just a decade ago.
  • The population of those 65+ is projected to grow from 852 million in 2025 to 2 billion in 2060.

5. 🧠 Brain implants fuel China rivalry
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Brain implants like those being developed by Elon Musk's Neuralink are becoming the latest friction point in the intensifying U.S.-China rivalry in the life sciences, Axios' Adriel Bettelheim writes.

  • Why it matters: The devices are bringing new hope to patients with strokes, Parkinson's disease and other neurological conditions. And tech billionaires have fueled advances by pouring billions into biotech startups focused on linking the brain with computers.

But a new national security analysis says U.S. development efforts are being overtaken by Beijing's full-court press around manufacturing, data and commercialization.

  • The consequences could extend beyond health care, affecting U.S. military capabilities and the ability to train the next generation of AI models, according to the analysis.

🔬 Zoom in: Brain-computer interfaces are going mainstream. Companies like Neuralink, Precision Neuroscience, Paradromics and Synchron are testing new applications, like helping to restore communication for people who have lost the ability to speak.

  • Rapid advances in artificial intelligence are reducing the time it takes to calibrate a device to a patient's brain signals and use them for functions like controlling a prosthetic part.
  • And China leveled up the field this spring, when it issued what's thought to be the world's first commercial approval of a brain-computer interface designed to revive hand movement in people with spinal cord injuries.

6. 👀 Witkoff meets powerful UAE official
 
Vessels sit near the Strait of Hormuz along the coast of Oman this week. Photo: Reuters

White House envoy Steve Witkoff met last weekend with the national security adviser of the United Arab Emirates to discuss next steps on Iran, Axios' Barak Ravid writes.

  • Witkoff met with Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan (TBZ) on the Mediterranean island of Sardinia.

Why it matters: The talks, which weren't announced by the White House and haven't been reported until now, took place amid the Trump administration's push to reopen the Strait of Hormuz while choking Iran economically.

  • The UAE has been the key partner in the U.S.-led operation to reopen and guide oil tankers through the strait.

7. 🏛️ Leadership power play fuels Dem infighting
 

Photo illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Photo: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
 

House Democratic leaders are trying to flex some muscle this week after two members defected on a key procedural vote. It's stoking fury among members across the political spectrum, Axios' Andrew Solender writes.

  • Why it matters: The blowup offers a preview of the chaos that party leaders could face in January if they take back the House majority.

At the same time, an effort to give House Democratic leaders more tools to keep their members in line next year is falling flat among rank-and-file members.

  • "It'll be dead by next week," predicted one senior House Democrat, speaking to Axios on the condition of anonymity to comment candidly on the maneuver.

🔭 Zoom in: Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) angered fellow Democrats on Tuesday by helping Republicans pass a rule, or procedural measure.

  • Some members have suggested kicking both members off their committees, or at least removing Gluesenkamp Perez from the powerful House Appropriations Committee.
  • Others have pitched a broader change to caucus rules requiring members to show up to key votes, stick with party leadership on rule votes and pay their dues to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

8. 🎾 1 for the road: Influencer reckoning
 
Fans take photos at the US Open last week. Photo: Manuela Davies/USTA via Getty Images

The U.S. Open has long been a "see and be seen" destination for fashion, business and Hollywood. Now, a growing class of content creators is joining the crowd — and getting schooled in tennis etiquette in real time, Axios Communicators author Simon Hernandez-Arthur writes.

  • One incident during Naomi Osaka's first-round match — where a group in a suite was taking photos with flash while Osaka was preparing to serve — prompted a public rebuke from the umpire.
  • Axios' Kerry Flynn, who's attended the U.S. Open every year since 2015, notes the etiquette has never felt this bad. It's always been rowdier than other tennis tournaments, but the party atmosphere has bled more into actual play.

🤳 Zoom out: The incident comes as the United States Tennis Association leans further into the creator economy. It approved credentials for "close to 100" content creators this year — nearly double the 54 it credentialed when it launched the program in 2025.

  • USTA media operations director Jeanmarie Daly told Front Office Sports the goal is to reach the "broadest possible spectrum" of audiences, recognizing that traditional media and creators reach people differently.
